full_title: ANTONIO R. CRUZ AND LORETO TERESITA CRUZ-DIMAYACYAC, AS HEIRS OF THE LATE SPOUSES DR. PROGEDIO R. CRUZ AND TERESA REYES, PETITIONERS, VS. CARLING CERVANTES AND CELIA CERVANTES SANTOS AND ALL PERSONS CLAIMING RIGHTS UNDER THEM, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: V. Special Civil Actions > J. Forcible Entry and Unlawful Detainer (Rule 70)
topics: Ejectment vs. agrarian dispute: jurisdiction of the MTC
Mandatory referral to the DAR under Section 50-A of RA 6657 (as added by RA 9700)
Kind of proof needed to show that a party is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant
Courts not bound by a DAR/PARO certification that states no findings of fact
Proof of agricultural tenancy (consent and sharing of harvest)

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: X. Administrative Law > D. Judicial Review of Administrative Action > 1. Doctrine of Primary Jurisdiction

doctrine:
Under **Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as added by Section 19 of RA No. 9700**, the judge or prosecutor must automatically refer a case to the DAR when two requisites concur: (1) an allegation from any one or both parties that the case is agrarian in nature; and (2) one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. A mere allegation suffices for the first requisite, but the second must be proved (reiterating *Chailese Development Co. v. Dizon* and *Dayrit v. Norquillas*). The Court **clarified** that the proof required for the second requisite is **any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows that one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant**; a facial assessment is enough, so that the referral mechanism is not defeated by protracted proceedings in the referring court.

Courts must comply with the referral mechanism, but they are **not bound to accept the DAR's recommendation** where it clearly violates the procedure in DAR Administrative Order No. 03-11, which requires a summary investigation and a PARO certification that states the findings of fact on which it is based. Under Section 54 of RA No. 6657, DAR findings are final only if based on substantial evidence. **A PARO certification that states no factual basis does not bind the referring court, which must independently assess the evidence and determine its own jurisdiction.**

Reiterated: occupancy and cultivation of agricultural land, no matter how long, do not make one a de jure tenant. There must be independent and concrete evidence of personal cultivation, sharing of harvest, and the landowner's consent, and receipt of produce without an agreed system of sharing does not create tenancy. Absent a tenancy relationship, the ejectment case remains within the MTC's jurisdiction.
facts:
Petitioners, heirs of the spouses Progedio and Teresa Cruz, filed a complaint for unlawful detainer dated February 22, 2016 with the MTC of Plaridel, Bulacan against respondents Carling Cervantes and Celia Cervantes Santos. They alleged that in 1960 Teresa allowed respondents' father Isidro to temporarily occupy a portion of their 2,702.10-square-meter lot in Bintog, Plaridel and build a house, on condition that his family would vacate upon demand. After the spouses died (1966 and 1999) and Isidro died (2005), respondents continued to occupy the property by tolerance. Petitioners revoked their tolerance by demand letter dated October 20, 2015, giving respondents 15 days to vacate; respondents refused. Petitioners also asked for PHP 5,000.00 monthly rentals.

In their Answer dated March 11, 2016, respondents claimed the land was agricultural and that they had succeeded to the tenancy rights of Isidro, who cultivated the land from 1965 to 2005 and planted camote, palay, vegetables, and fruit trees. They attached a rice mill tally sheet with the entry "Name: Mrs. Teresa Reyes Vda de Cruz; Kasama: Isidro Cervante[s]" and a handwritten receipt dated March 31, 1992 reading "Buwis sa Bakuran x x x ni Sidro Cervantes." Petitioners denied any tenancy: respondents occupied only about 300 square meters, and no crops were planted on the land.

In an Order dated March 29, 2016, the MTC referred the case to the Provincial Agrarian Reform Office (PARO) under RA No. 6657, as amended by RA No. 9700, and OCA Circular No. 62-10. On October 28, 2016, the PARO certified that the case was agrarian in nature "for it involves an agricultural land and the cause of action is ejectment of a farmer, farmworker or tenant," and recommended dismissal. The MTC dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction on February 9, 2017. The RTC of Malolos (Branch 15) affirmed on February 28, 2018, and the CA affirmed on September 27, 2018 (CA-G.R. SP No. 155023), denying reconsideration on January 21, 2019. Petitioners filed a Rule 45 petition, arguing among others that the dismissal relied merely on the PARO certification without affording them a hearing.
issues: Whether the MTC correctly referred the unlawful detainer case to the DAR (through the PARO) under Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as amended.
Whether the MTC correctly dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction by relying on the PARO certification that the case is agrarian in nature.
Whether respondents proved an agricultural tenancy relationship that would place the case within the DAR's jurisdiction.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the referral was proper.** Section 50-A requires automatic referral when (1) a party alleges that the case is agrarian in nature, and (2) one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. Following *Chailese* and *Dayrit*, a simple allegation suffices for the first requisite, but adequate proof is needed for the second. The law is silent on the kind of proof, so the Court held that it "shall pertain to any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows that one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant". A higher standard would prolong proceedings in the referring court and defeat the purpose of letting the DAR, with its expertise, determine the nature of the dispute. Respondents' answer and its annexes (the tally sheet and the receipt) supported, on their face, the claim that Isidro was a tenant, so the MTC did not err in referring the case.

**2. No, the MTC erred in adopting the PARO certification.** DAR AO No. 03-11 requires the PARO to conduct a summary investigation, receive the parties' evidence and position papers, and issue a certification that "shall state the findings of fact upon which the determination by the PARO was based." The PARO certification here only stated its conclusion and gave no findings of fact, leaving the courts "with no basis to ascertain the evidence from which its findings were drawn." **While courts must comply with the referral mechanism, "they are not bound to accept the recommendation where such determination clearly violated the procedures and requirements set forth by DAR AO 03-11."** The referring court must independently assess the DAR's recommendation in light of the evidence. Administrative findings of fact deserve respect, but under Section 54 of RA No. 6657 they are final only when based on substantial evidence. Where the administrative body fails to state the basis of its findings or misappreciates the evidence, courts may disregard them.

**3. No tenancy was proved, so the MTC has jurisdiction.** The tally sheet naming Isidro as "Kasama" and the receipt for "Buwis sa Bakuran" did not show that the spouses Cruz consented to a tenancy relationship or agreed to share the harvest. "[O]ccupancy and cultivation of an agricultural land, no matter how long, will not ipso facto make one a de jure tenant"; independent and concrete evidence of personal cultivation, sharing of harvest, or the landowner's consent is necessary, and the tenant must show that he delivered the landowner's share. Citing *Rivera v. Santiago*, mere receipt of produce without an agreed sharing system does not create tenancy. Respondents failed to discharge their burden, so **the complaint remains an ordinary ejectment case within the MTC's jurisdiction.**
disposition: The petition was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated September 27, 2018 and Resolution dated January 21, 2019 in CA-G.R. SP No. 155023 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE, and the case was REMANDED to the MTC of Plaridel, Bulacan for further proceedings.

bar_questions.q: The spouses Abad own a 2,000-square-meter lot in Bulacan. In 1990 they allowed Celso to build a house on a portion of it, on condition that he would leave upon demand. In 2024 they demanded that he vacate, and when he refused, they filed an unlawful detainer complaint with the MTC. In his answer, Celso alleged that the case is agrarian because he is their tenant, and attached a rice mill tally sheet listing him as "kasama" of Mrs. Abad. The MTC referred the case to the PARO. The PARO issued a one-paragraph certification that the case is agrarian in nature because it involves agricultural land and the ejectment of a tenant, and it recommended dismissal. The certification states no findings of fact. Relying on it, the MTC dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction. Was the dismissal proper?

alac.answer: No. The referral was proper, but the MTC erred in dismissing the complaint on the strength of a PARO certification that states no findings of fact.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as added by Section 19 of RA No. 9700, a court must refer a case to the DAR when a party alleges that it is agrarian in nature and one party is shown to be a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. DAR AO No. 03-11 requires the PARO to conduct a summary investigation and to state in its certification the findings of fact on which it is based. Courts must comply with the referral mechanism but are not bound to accept a recommendation that clearly violates DAR AO No. 03-11; they must independently assess it in light of the evidence. Under Section 54 of RA No. 6657, DAR findings are final only if based on substantial evidence. (Cruz v. Cervantes, G.R. No. 244433, April 19, 2022)
alac.application: Celso alleged that the case is agrarian and attached a tally sheet that, on its face, tends to show he is a tenant, so the MTC correctly referred the case. But the PARO certification states only a conclusion. It gives no findings of fact, so the court has no way to tell what evidence supports it. The MTC could not simply adopt it. It had to assess the evidence itself and determine whether a tenancy relationship exists and, therefore, whether it has jurisdiction.
alac.conclusion: The dismissal was improper; the MTC must make its own determination of jurisdiction instead of relying on a certification without factual basis.

bar_questions.q: In an unlawful detainer case before the MTC, defendant Dario states in his answer, without attaching any document, that "this case is agrarian in nature and I am the agricultural tenant of the plaintiff." (a) Is the MTC required to refer the case to the DAR? (b) Would your answer be the same if Dario had attached a handwritten receipt signed by the plaintiff acknowledging delivery of the landowner's share of the palay harvest?

alac.answer: (a) No. A bare allegation that he is a tenant does not satisfy the second requisite for mandatory referral. (b) No, the answer would be different: the receipt is evidence which on its face shows that Dario is a tenant, so the MTC must refer the case.
alac.legal_basis: Referral to the DAR under Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as amended by RA No. 9700, is mandatory when two requisites concur: (1) an allegation that the case is agrarian in nature, and (2) one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. A simple allegation suffices for the first requisite, but adequate proof is necessary for the second. The proof required is any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows that one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. (Cruz v. Cervantes, G.R. No. 244433, April 19, 2022, reiterating Chailese Development Co. v. Dizon)
alac.application: (a) Dario's statement that the case is agrarian satisfies the first requisite. But his claim that he is a tenant is only an allegation with no supporting proof, so the second requisite is not met and the MTC may proceed with the ejectment case. (b) A receipt signed by the landowner acknowledging delivery of her share of the harvest is evidence that, on a facial assessment, a reasonable mind would accept as showing that Dario is a tenant. The MTC need not and should not try the tenancy issue in full before referring. Both requisites are then present, and the MTC must refer the case.
alac.conclusion: Referral is not required on a bare allegation of tenancy, but it becomes mandatory once Dario presents evidence that on its face shows he is a tenant.

bar_questions.q: Ramon has occupied and cultivated a portion of Lourdes's agricultural land for 30 years, planting vegetables and fruit trees. When Lourdes sued to eject him, Ramon claimed to be her agricultural tenant. His only evidence is (1) a rice mill tally sheet naming him as "kasama" of Lourdes's late mother and (2) a 1995 receipt for "buwis sa bakuran." (a) Has Ramon proved a tenancy relationship? (b) If the MTC had referred the case to the DAR and the PARO had certified that it is agrarian, what judicial recourse would Lourdes have against that determination, and in which court?

alac.answer: (a) No. Long occupancy and cultivation, a tally sheet, and a receipt for "buwis sa bakuran" do not prove the landowner's consent to a tenancy or an agreed sharing of the harvest. (b) Lourdes may seek judicial recourse from the DAR's determination; since the case was referred by the MTC, the appeal lies with the proper RTC.
alac.legal_basis: Occupancy and cultivation of agricultural land, no matter how long, do not make one a de jure tenant. Independent and concrete evidence is needed to prove personal cultivation, sharing of harvest, or consent of the landowner, and the tenant must show that he delivered the landowner's share. Receipt of produce without an agreed system of sharing does not create tenancy. (Cruz v. Cervantes, G.R. No. 244433, April 19, 2022, citing Rivera v. Santiago) Section 50-A of RA No. 6657, as amended by RA No. 9700, provides that from the DAR's determination "an aggrieved party shall have judicial recourse," and that in cases referred by the MTC "the appeal shall be with the proper regional trial court."
alac.application: (a) Ramon's 30 years of occupancy and cultivation do not by themselves make him a tenant. The tally sheet and the 1995 receipt, as in Cruz, do not show that Lourdes or her mother consented to a tenancy relationship or agreed to share the harvest, and nothing shows he delivered a landowner's share. Ramon has not discharged his burden, so the case remains an ejectment case for the MTC. (b) If the PARO certifies that the case is agrarian, Lourdes is not without remedy. Since the MTC was the referring court, she may appeal the DAR's determination to the proper RTC. And the MTC itself is not bound by a determination that lacks factual basis or is unsupported by substantial evidence.
alac.conclusion: Ramon has not proved tenancy, and Lourdes may elevate an adverse DAR determination to the proper RTC.

notes: Petitioners also argued that Section 19 of RA No. 9700 and OCA Circular No. 62-10 are unconstitutional; the main opinion did not rule on that argument and decided the case on the grounds above. The "facial evidence" standard for the second requisite was drawn from Justice Caguioa's concurring opinion but was expressly adopted by the Court in the main opinion ("As such, We hold that the proof required shall pertain to any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows..."). The concurring opinions of Perlas-Bernabe, Leonen, Caguioa, and Lazaro-Javier, JJ. were not used for the doctrine.
